questions.prompt: What do you do when you are travelling on public transport?

vocabulary.title: Q1 - What You Do on Public Transport
phrases: catch up on messages and emails
sentenceStarters: My behaviour on public transport has changed quite significantly...
I also use the time to catch up on messages and emails...
I think the commute is an underappreciated opportunity...

questions.sampleBand5: Well, um, usually I just listen to music. Or, sometimes I just, like, zone out and look out the window. It's, um, pretty boring most of the time, yeah.
questions.sampleBand6: Um, generally, I listen to music on my phone, or sometimes I try to read a book. It really depends on how crowded it is, to be honest. If it's too packed, reading is impossible. I just end up staring into space. It's not ideal but, yeah.
questions.sampleBand7: Well, I usually try to make the most of the time. I mean, I often listen to podcasts or audiobooks. Or, if I have some work to do, I might try to catch up on emails. Every now and then, I'll just people-watch, which can be surprisingly entertaining, actually. As long as I can block out the noise!
questions.sampleBand8: When I'm travelling on public transport, I try to use the time productively. I often listen to podcasts related to my field, which helps me stay up-to-date. Or, if I'm not feeling that ambitious, I might read a book or scroll through social media. It's also a good opportunity to just relax and switch off before arriving at my destination. Actually, I find it quite therapeutic sometimes.
questions.sampleBand9: Well, it really depends on the length of the journey, but I try to make the most of it. If it's a short trip, I might just catch up on the news or listen to a quick podcast. However, on longer journeys, I often use the time to read, or even work if I can get a seat. I find it’s a good opportunity to clear my head and prepare for the day ahead, or unwind after a long day at work. Ultimately, I see it as a chance to be productive, or simply to zone out and enjoy the ride.
questions.sampleAnswer: My behaviour on public transport has changed quite significantly over the years, and I think it reflects broader shifts in how people use commuting time. I used to read physical books or newspapers—there was something about the enforced stillness of a train or bus journey that made it a good time for sustained reading. Now I'm more likely to listen to podcasts or audiobooks, which I find works well because it doesn't require the same level of visual attention and can continue even when the journey is crowded or uncomfortable. I also use the time to catch up on messages and emails, though I try to be selective about this—I find that spending an entire commute on a phone can leave you feeling more depleted than refreshed. Occasionally, when I'm not doing anything in particular, I find that public transport journeys are actually quite good for thinking—the slight detachment from your normal environment, combined with the rhythm of movement, can create a mental state that's conducive to reflection and problem-solving. I think the commute is an underappreciated opportunity for the kind of unstructured thinking that is increasingly rare in a world of constant connectivity.

questions.uzSampleBand8: Men jamoat transportida sayohat qilganimda, vaqtdan unumli foydalanishga harakat qilaman. Yoki, agar men o'zimni bunchalik g'ayratli his qilmasam, kitob o'qishim yoki ijtimoiy tarmoqlarni varaqlashim mumkin. Bu shuningdek, manzilimga yetib kelishdan oldin shunchaki dam olish va o'chirish uchun yaxshi imkoniyat. Aslida, men buni ba'zan juda davolovchi deb bilaman.
questions.uzSampleBand9: Xo'sh, bu sayohatning uzunligiga bog'liq, lekin men undan unumli foydalanishga harakat qilaman. Agar bu qisqa sayohat bo'lsa, men shunchaki yangiliklarni ko'rib chiqishim yoki tezkor podkastni tinglashim mumkin. Biroq, uzoqroq sayohatlarda, men ko'pincha o'qish uchun vaqt ajrataman, yoki hatto o'tirishga joy topsam, ishlayman. Menimcha, bu miyamni tozalash va kunni kutib olishga tayyorgarlik ko'rish yoki ishda uzoq kundan keyin dam olish uchun yaxshi imkoniyat. Oxir-oqibat, men buni unumli bo'lish, yoki shunchaki o'ylanib qolish va sayohatdan zavqlanish imkoniyati sifatida ko'raman.
questions.uzSampleAnswer: Jamoat transportida o'zimni tutishim yillar davomida ancha o'zgardi va menimcha, bu odamlarning qatnov vaqtidan qanday foydalanishida kengroq o'zgarishlarni aks ettiradi. Ilgari men kitoblar yoki gazetalar o'qirdim — poyezd yoki avtobusda majburiy sokinlik uzoq vaqt o'qish uchun yaxshi vaqt bo'lardi. Hozir men ko'proq podkastlar yoki audiokitoblarni tinglayman, chunki bu ko'rishga unchalik e'tibor talab qilmaydi va hatto sayohat olomon yoki noqulay bo'lganda ham davom etishi mumkin. Shuningdek, men vaqtni xabarlar va elektron pochta xabarlarini ko'rib chiqish uchun ishlataman, lekin bu borada tanlab harakat qilishga harakat qilaman — butun qatnov vaqtini telefonda o'tkazish sizni tetiklashdan ko'ra ko'proq charchagan his qilishingizga olib kelishi mumkin. Ba'zida, men hech narsa qilmayotganimda, jamoat transportida sayohatlar aslida o'ylash uchun juda yaxshi ekanligini bilaman — odatiy muhitingizdan biroz ajralish, harakat ritmi bilan birgalikda, fikrlash va muammolarni hal qilishga yordam beradigan ruhiy holatni yaratishi mumkin. Menimcha, qatnov doimiy bog'liqlik dunyosida tobora kamayib borayotgan tuzilmagan fikrlash uchun kam baholangan imkoniyatdir.

questions.prompt: How could public transport in your country be improved?

vocabulary.title: Q2 - Improving Public Transport
phrases: cost too high relative to driving
sentenceStarters: Public transport in my country has genuine strengths but also...
The most fundamental improvement would be reliability...
I also think the cost of public transport in many countries...

questions.sampleBand5: Well, um, I think the buses, heavy traffic is a problem. More buses, maybe? And, um, pick up people more often. I'm not sure, really. Need more trains too.
questions.sampleBand6: I think honestly, public transport in my country needs a lot of work. The buses are often late, and the trains are overcrowded. Maybe investing in more frequent services would help. Also, improving the road network could reduce delays for buses, I suppose. It's a tough problem.
questions.sampleBand7: Well, public transport in my country could definitely be improved. Firstly, the reliability is a major issue; buses and trains are often delayed or cancelled. Investing in better infrastructure, like dedicated bus lanes, would help. Furthermore, the ticketing system is quite outdated; a unified, digital system would cut down on queues and make things much easier for commuters. It's a real pain point for many.
questions.sampleBand8: I think there are several ways public transport could be improved. For example, a significant investment in expanding the rail network would be beneficial, particularly in rural areas that are currently underserved. Moreover, integrating different modes of transport, such as buses and trains, with a single ticketing system would make commuting much more convenient. It's all about making public transport a more attractive alternative to driving, which would also cut down on congestion. The key issue is funding and long-term planning.
questions.sampleBand9: Public transport in my country has significant room for improvement. Firstly, a comprehensive overhaul of the infrastructure is needed, including modernizing the existing rail network and expanding bus routes to cater to underserved communities. Secondly, a fully integrated, user-friendly ticketing system, perhaps leveraging mobile technology, would streamline the passenger experience. However, it's not just about infrastructure; a shift in mindset is also required. We need to move away from viewing public transport as a last resort and towards seeing it as a viable, attractive, and even preferable option. In the long run, this requires a multi-faceted approach involving government investment, technological innovation, and a commitment to sustainability. It's a tall order, but it's essential for creating a more livable and sustainable future.
questions.sampleAnswer: Public transport in my country has genuine strengths but also significant weaknesses, and I think the improvements that would make the most difference are fairly clear even if the political will to implement them is sometimes lacking. The most fundamental improvement would be reliability—the gap between the scheduled and actual performance of trains and buses is often significant, and unreliability is probably the single biggest deterrent to public transport use. People can tolerate crowding and cost to a greater extent than they can tolerate unpredictability—if you can't rely on a service to get you somewhere on time, you'll use a car instead. Extending coverage to underserved areas—particularly rural communities and outer suburbs—would also make a significant difference. The integration of different modes of transport is another area for improvement—the experience of seamlessly moving between train, bus, and cycling infrastructure is much better in some countries than in others, and better integration would make public transport more competitive with the car for complex journeys. I also think the cost of public transport in many countries is too high relative to driving, which creates a perverse incentive that works against environmental goals. Making public transport cheaper—ideally free for certain groups—would significantly increase uptake.
questions.uzSampleBand5: Xo'sh, mm, menimcha, avtobuslar, tirbandlik muammo. Ko'proq avtobuslar, balki? Va, mm, odamlarni tez-tez olib ketish. Aniq emasman, rostini aytsam. Ko'proq poyezdlar ham kerak.
questions.uzSampleBand6: Men ochig'ini aytsam, mening mamlakatimdagi jamoat transporti ko'p ishlarni talab qiladi deb o'ylayman. Avtobuslar ko'pincha kech qoladi, poyezdlar esa tiqilib ketgan. Balki tez-tez xizmat ko'rsatishga sarmoya kiritish yordam berar. Bundan tashqari, yo'l tarmog'ini yaxshilash avtobuslar uchun kechikishlarni kamaytirishi mumkin, deb o'ylayman. Bu qiyin muammo.
questions.uzSampleBand7: Xo'sh, mening mamlakatimdagi jamoat transportini albatta yaxshilash mumkin. Birinchidan, ishonchlilik asosiy muammo; avtobuslar va poyezdlar ko'pincha kechikadi yoki bekor qilinadi. Yaxshiroq infratuzilmaga, masalan, avtobuslar uchun alohida yo'laklarga sarmoya kiritish yordam beradi. Bundan tashqari, chipta tizimi juda eskirgan; yagona, raqamli tizim navbatlarni qisqartiradi va qatnovchilar uchun ishni ancha osonlashtiradi. Bu ko'pchilik uchun haqiqiy og'riqli nuqta.
questions.uzSampleBand8: Menimcha, jamoat transportini yaxshilashning bir necha yo'li bor. Misol uchun, temir yo'l tarmog'ini kengaytirishga katta sarmoya kiritish foydali bo'ladi, ayniqsa, hozirda xizmat ko'rsatilmagan qishloq joylarda. Bundan tashqari, avtobuslar va poyezdlar kabi transportning turli usullarini yagona chipta tizimi bilan integratsiyalash qatnovni ancha qulay qiladi. Gap shundaki, jamoat transportini haydashga nisbatan jozibadorroq alternativaga aylantirish, bu esa tirbandlikni ham qisqartiradi. Asosiy masala moliyalashtirish va uzoq muddatli rejalashtirish.
questions.uzSampleBand9: Mening mamlakatimdagi jamoat transportini yaxshilash uchun sezilarli imkoniyatlar mavjud. Birinchidan, infratuzilmani har tomonlama ta'mirlash kerak, jumladan, mavjud temir yo'l tarmog'ini modernizatsiya qilish va xizmat ko'rsatilmagan hududlarga avtobus yo'nalishlarini kengaytirish. Ikkinchidan, to'liq integratsiyalashgan, foydalanuvchilar uchun qulay chipta tizimi, ehtimol mobil texnologiyalardan foydalangan holda, yo'lovchi tajribasini soddalashtiradi. Biroq, gap faqat infratuzilmada emas; fikrlash tarzida ham o'zgarish talab etiladi. Biz jamoat transportiga so'nggi chora sifatida qarashdan uzaqlashishimiz va unga hayotiy, jozibali va hatto afzalroq variant sifatida qarashga o'tishimiz kerak. Uzoq muddatda bu hukumat sarmoyasi, texnologik innovatsiyalar va barqarorlikka sodiqlikni o'z ichiga olgan ko'p qirrali yondashuvni talab qiladi. Bu qiyin vazifa, lekin bu yanada yashashga yaroqli va barqaror kelajakni yaratish uchun zarurdir.
questions.uzSampleAnswer: Mening mamlakatimdagi jamoat transporti ba'zi kuchli tomonlarga ega, lekin sezilarli kamchiliklari ham bor va menimcha, eng katta o'zgarishlarni keltiradigan yaxshilanishlar ancha aniq, hatto ularni amalga oshirish uchun siyosiy iroda ba'zan yetishmasa ham. Eng asosiy yaxshilanish - bu ishonchlilik bo'ladi - poyezdlar va avtobuslarning rejalashtirilgan va amaldagi ishlashi o'rtasidagi farq ko'pincha sezilarli va ishonchsizlik, ehtimol, jamoat transportidan foydalanishga eng katta to'siqdir. Odamlar olomon va xarajatlarga chidashi mumkin, lekin oldindan aytib bo'lmaslikka emas - agar siz xizmatga bir joyga o'z vaqtida yetib borish uchun ishonchingiz komil bo'lmasa, uning o'rniga mashinadan foydalanasiz. Xizmat ko'rsatilmagan hududlarga, ayniqsa, qishloq jamoalari va chekka shaharlarga qamrovni kengaytirish ham sezilarli o'zgarishlar qiladi. Transportning turli usullarini integratsiyalashuvi yaxshilanish uchun yana bir soha - poyezd, avtobus va velosiped infratuzilmasi o'rtasida uzluksiz harakatlanish tajribasi ba'zi mamlakatlarda boshqalarga qaraganda ancha yaxshi va yaxshiroq integratsiya jamoat transportini murakkab sayohatlar uchun mashina bilan raqobatbardosh qiladi. Menimcha, ko'plab mamlakatlarda jamoat transportining narxi haydashga nisbatan juda yuqori, bu esa atrof-muhit maqsadlariga qarshi ishlaydigan teskari rag'bat yaratadi. Jamoat transportini arzonlashtirish - ideal holda, ma'lum guruhlar uchun bepul qilish - qamrovni sezilarli darajada oshiradi.

questions.sampleAnswer: If I'm being honest about what I actually enjoy rather than what I merely tolerate, trains are my favourite form of public transport by a significant margin. Long-distance train journeys in particular have a quality of adventure and contemplation that I associate with some of my best travel experiences. There's also the practical dimension—trains are generally faster and more comfortable than buses for longer journeys, and the ability to move around, to visit a dining car, or simply to stand and stretch makes them more pleasant for extended travel. I also appreciate the environmental dimension—trains are significantly more carbon-efficient than flying or driving, which makes choosing them feel like a responsible decision as well as a pleasant one. I think the experience of train travel varies enormously by country—some countries have invested heavily in high-speed rail and offer a genuinely world-class experience, while others have allowed their rail networks to deteriorate.

questions.uzSampleAnswer: Agar rostini aytsam, shunchaki chidab bo'ladigan narsalardan ko'ra, menga haqiqatan ham yoqadigan narsa haqida gapiradigan bo'lsam, poyezdlar mening eng sevimli jamoat transporti vositamdir. Poyezdda sayohat qilishda shunday bir narsa borki, men avtobus yoki metroda sayohat qilishda kamdan-kam hollarda topadigan zavqni topaman - tezlik, derazadan ko'rinish, haqiqiy masofani bosib o'tish hissi va poyezddan ko'rish mumkin bo'lgan yorug'lik va landshaftning o'ziga xos sifati menga haqiqatan ham yoqadigan narsalardir. Ayniqsa, uzoq masofali poyezd safarlari sarguzasht va mulohaza sifatiga ega, buni men eng yaxshi sayohat tajribalarim bilan bog'layman. Amaliy jihati ham bor - poyezdlar uzoqroq safarlar uchun avtobuslarga qaraganda tezroq va qulayroq, harakatlanish, ovqatlanish vagoniga tashrif buyurish yoki shunchaki turib cho'zilish imkoniyati ularni uzoqroq safarlar uchun yanada yoqimli qiladi. fast fashion and global supply chains
sentenceStarters: The seasonal variation in clothing in my country is quite pronounced...
The transitional seasons—spring and autumn—are interesting...
I think the seasonal variation in clothing is one of the more visible ways...

questions.sampleBand5: Well, um, basically, in my country, people wear different clothes. In summer, it's hot, so they wear shorts. And, um, in winter, it's cold, so they wear coats. Yeah, simple clothes.
questions.sampleBand6: Um, well, the clothes people wear here depend on the season, of course. Like, in the summer, people tend to wear lighter clothes, like t-shirts and shorts, because it gets really hot. Then, in the winter, it's the opposite; everyone bundles up in thick coats and scarves.
questions.sampleBand7: Okay, so, the way people dress in my country definitely changes depending on the time of year. During the summer months, when it's really hot and humid, you'll see people wearing light, breathable fabrics like cotton and linen. On the other hand, when winter rolls around, people tend to wear a lot more layers to keep warm, so you'll see a lot of wool and heavier materials.
questions.sampleBand8: Well, obviously, there's a significant shift in clothing styles throughout the year. During the hotter months, lightweight and breathable fabrics are really popular; things like linen and cotton become wardrobe staples. As soon as the temperature starts to drop, though, people break out the heavier jackets, sweaters, and scarves. Actually, you can sort of tell the season just by looking at what people are wearing on the street.
questions.sampleBand9: The change in seasons dictates a pretty dramatic shift in wardrobes across the country. During the sweltering summer months, practicality reigns supreme, with people favouring loose-fitting, breathable garments to combat the heat and humidity. Conversely, winter sees a wholesale adoption of warmer, more insulating fabrics. People layer up with wool, down, and other materials designed to ward off the often harsh conditions. It's quite noticeable, really, and reflects the country's diverse climate.
questions.sampleAnswer: The seasonal variation in clothing in my country is quite pronounced, reflecting the significant differences in temperature and weather between summer and winter. In summer, people dress for warmth and informality—lighter fabrics, shorter sleeves, open footwear—and there's a general loosening of dress codes that reflects the more relaxed atmosphere of the warmer months. In winter, the emphasis shifts to warmth and layering—heavier coats, boots, scarves, and hats become standard, and the colour palette tends to darken as people move toward more muted, autumnal tones. The transitional seasons—spring and autumn—are interesting because the unpredictability of the weather creates a kind of sartorial uncertainty—you might need a coat in the morning and find yourself too warm by the afternoon. I think the seasonal variation in clothing is one of the more visible ways in which the seasons shape daily life—the wardrobe itself changes significantly, and the ritual of transitioning between seasonal wardrobes is something many people find either satisfying or burdensome depending on their relationship with clothing. I also think the relationship between fashion and season has become more complex with the rise of fast fashion and global supply chains, which have made seasonal clothing available year-round.

questions.sampleAnswer: Yes, seasonal employment is a significant feature of the labour market in my country, and the pattern of seasonal work reflects the structure of the economy and the climate. The tourism and hospitality sector is also strongly seasonal—coastal resorts, ski resorts, and tourist attractions in scenic areas employ significantly more people during the peak tourist season than at other times of year. Construction work is also affected by the seasons, though less dramatically—outdoor construction is more difficult in winter, and some projects are scheduled to take advantage of better weather. Retail employment spikes significantly in the run-up to Christmas and other major shopping periods. I think seasonal employment raises interesting questions about labour market flexibility and worker security—seasonal workers often lack the job security and benefits of permanent employees, and the seasonal nature of their work can make financial planning difficult. The rise of the gig economy has in some ways formalised and extended the logic of seasonal employment, creating a larger pool of workers who move between short-term engagements rather than holding permanent positions.

Coastal areas and rural destinations with scenic landscapes are particularly popular during this period. However, certain types of tourism are specifically associated with other seasons—winter tourism is significant in areas with ski resorts, and there's a growing market for autumn tourism in regions with spectacular autumn foliage. City tourism tends to be less seasonal than rural or coastal tourism—major cities attract visitors year-round, though they also have peak periods around major events and holidays. I think the concentration of tourism in a single season creates both opportunities and challenges—it generates significant economic activity during the peak period but can put considerable strain on infrastructure and natural environments. There's a growing recognition in the tourism industry of the value of spreading visitor numbers more evenly across the year, and many destinations are actively promoting off-season tourism to address this.

There's something about the quality of autumn light and the slight chill in the air that I find conducive to concentration and sustained effort. I think this may be partly cultural—the academic year in many countries begins in autumn, which creates an association between that season and focused work—but I also think there's something more fundamental about the way cooler temperatures and shorter days encourage a kind of inward focus that is helpful for intellectual work. Research on the relationship between income and wellbeing consistently shows that beyond the point where your basic needs and a reasonable level of comfort are met, additional income has diminishing returns in terms of life satisfaction. What continues to matter is the quality of your work—whether it feels meaningful, whether you have autonomy and mastery, whether you're part of a community of people you respect. I also think the framing of 'love' is somewhat misleading—most people don't love their jobs in the way they love their families or their hobbies, and expecting to is probably unrealistic. The more achievable goal is work that you find genuinely interesting, that aligns with your values, and that you can do with a degree of competence and pride.

questions.sampleAnswer: Job security is genuinely important to me, though I think its importance is somewhat contextual—it matters more at certain life stages and in certain circumstances than others. At earlier life stages, when your financial obligations are lighter and your skills are more transferable, the value of job security relative to other factors—interesting work, learning opportunities, career development—is somewhat lower. I also think the concept of job security has become more complex in the contemporary labour market, where the idea of a job for life has largely disappeared and where the security of employment is more about the transferability of your skills than about the stability of any particular position. In this sense, I think the most meaningful form of job security is not security in a specific job but security in your ability to find work—which comes from having skills that are genuinely valued, a strong professional network, and a track record of achievement. I try to think about security in these terms rather than in terms of the stability of my current position.

questions.sampleAnswer: Children's job preferences are fascinating because they reveal a combination of genuine values and the influence of cultural messaging, and they change significantly as children develop and encounter a wider range of possibilities. As children get older, their preferences become more influenced by their own experiences, their perceived strengths, and the careers they see modelled by the adults around them. There's also a significant influence from popular culture—jobs that are glamorised in films, television, and social media attract disproportionate interest. The rise of social media has created a new category of aspirational career—content creator, influencer, YouTuber—that didn't exist a generation ago and that now features prominently in surveys of children's career aspirations. I think what's most interesting about children's job preferences is that they often reflect a desire for meaning and impact that gets somewhat lost in the more pragmatic career choices of adulthood.

questions.sampleAnswer: I think the research on this question is fairly clear, even if it runs counter to some people's intuitions: beyond a certain income threshold, interest and meaning matter significantly more than salary for long-term job satisfaction and overall wellbeing. The classic research by Kahneman and Deaton suggested that emotional wellbeing increases with income up to a certain point—roughly the level at which your basic needs and a reasonable standard of living are secured—and then plateaus. Above that threshold, additional income has diminishing returns in terms of happiness, while the quality of your work—its meaningfulness, your level of autonomy, the relationships it involves—continues to matter. I think the practical implication of this is that people should prioritise interest and meaning once their income needs are met, and should be cautious about accepting significantly higher pay in exchange for work they find meaningless or environments they find toxic. The temptation to take a higher-paying job that you find less interesting is real and understandable, but the evidence suggests that most people adapt to higher income relatively quickly while the daily experience of doing work you find dull or alienating is harder to adapt to. That said, I think the framing of salary versus interest as a binary choice is somewhat misleading—the best outcome is to find work that is both well-compensated and genuinely interesting.

questions.sampleAnswer: Salary is certainly an important factor in job choice, but I don't think it's the main reason for most people in most circumstances—and the evidence from surveys of job satisfaction and career motivation supports this view. When people are asked what they value most in their work, salary typically appears in the top five but is rarely the most frequently cited factor. Things like meaningful work, good relationships with colleagues, opportunities for growth, autonomy, and a positive working environment consistently rank as highly or more highly than pay. I think the prominence of salary in discussions of career choice partly reflects the fact that it's the most easily quantifiable and comparable factor—you can compare salaries across jobs much more easily than you can compare the quality of working relationships or the degree of autonomy. This makes salary a convenient shorthand for job quality even when it's not the most important factor. I also think the importance of salary varies significantly by context—for people in lower-income brackets, where financial security is a genuine concern, salary is naturally a more pressing consideration than for those whose basic needs are already well met. And for people in certain professions—particularly those in the public sector or non-profit sector—the choice to accept lower pay in exchange for more meaningful work is a deliberate and considered decision.

questions.sampleBand9: The transformation in the nature of work over recent decades is, in my view, a profound one, driven primarily by technological innovation and the inexorable forces of globalization. The low-hanging fruit of routine tasks has been largely automated, demanding that individuals cultivate skills in areas like critical thinking, creativity, and complex problem-solving. Furthermore, the rise of the gig economy and remote work has blurred the traditional boundaries between work and personal life, creating both opportunities and challenges. questions.sampleAnswer: The nature of work has changed profoundly over the past few decades, driven by technological change, globalisation, and shifting cultural expectations about what work should provide and what workers should expect. The most dramatic change has probably been the shift from manufacturing to service and knowledge work in many developed economies—the proportion of people doing physical, manual labour has declined significantly, while the proportion doing cognitive, relational, and creative work has grown. Technology has transformed almost every sector—automation has eliminated many routine tasks while creating new categories of work, and digital tools have changed how almost all knowledge work is done. The rise of remote and flexible working—accelerated dramatically by the pandemic—has changed the relationship between work and place in ways that are still being worked out. The gig economy has created new forms of work that don't fit neatly into traditional categories of employment, raising important questions about worker rights and protections. I think the most significant long-term change is the increasing importance of continuous learning—the idea that you can acquire a set of skills in your twenties and use them for the rest of your working life is increasingly obsolete, and the ability to learn, adapt, and acquire new skills has become one of the most important qualities in the contemporary labour market.

questions.sampleAnswer: Yes, I think artificial intelligence will have a profound and transformative effect on the labour market, though the nature and extent of that transformation is genuinely uncertain and is the subject of significant debate among economists and technologists. The most immediate effect is already visible—AI is automating tasks that were previously thought to require human intelligence, including tasks in knowledge work and creative fields that were assumed to be safe from automation. This is different from previous waves of automation, which primarily affected routine physical tasks, because AI is increasingly capable of performing cognitive tasks that require pattern recognition, language processing, and even creative generation. The optimistic view is that AI will, like previous technological revolutions, create new categories of work even as it eliminates existing ones—that the productivity gains from AI will generate new economic activity and new jobs that we can't currently anticipate. The pessimistic view is that this time is different—that AI is capable of performing such a wide range of tasks that the displacement of workers will outpace the creation of new roles. I think the honest answer is that we don't know, but that the transition will be significant and will require serious investment in education, retraining, and social support systems to ensure that the benefits of AI are broadly shared rather than concentrated among a small number of people and organisations.
